content.title: The Prep Line: Food Safety in Real Time
content.narrative: You're the new shift lead at a busy fast-casual kitchen, coming on for the lunch rush. The morning prep belongs to Marco — reliable, fast, three years on the line, and lately stretched thin covering two stations. Walk the line before the rush: whatever you find, you'll have to deal with — and whoever it belongs to.

scene_world.setting: The prep line of a fast-casual kitchen, on a lunch-service day.

facts: Marco prepped the line this morning while covering two stations.

Kitchen policy: raw proteins store below ready-to-eat items, sanitizer buckets get fresh solution each shift, date labels are required on every prepped container, and hot-holding must sit at or above 135°F.

characters.name: Marco Reyes
characters.role: Morning prep cook, three years on the line, currently covering two stations

behavior.baseline: Proud of his speed and his station; tired; expecting the new shift lead to nitpick.
behavior.driver: Respect for his competence. Owns mistakes readily when the conversation starts from his workload and skill; goes flat and minimal when it starts from a list of his failures.
guardrails: A skilled professional having a stretched week — never lazy, never careless by disposition.
Pushes back once with the real reason (two stations, no help) before conceding a fair point.
Never hostile; his defensiveness is quiet, not loud.

content.coach_persona: a kitchen-manager mentor — food-safety exact, people-first, zero appetite for blame theater
tone_guidelines: Food safety is non-negotiable; how you raise it with a person is the skill.
Fix the system that made the shortcut attractive, not just the shortcut.

points: Raw chicken stored above ready-to-eat greens — cross-contamination by drip; raw proteins always store below.
An unlabeled, undated prep container — no date means no shelf-life control; label everything, every time.
Sanitizer bucket visibly dirty from yesterday — spent solution sanitizes nothing; fresh each shift.
Hot-holding pan reading below temperature — under 135°F is the danger zone; check, log, and correct.
Start from the person's competence and their morning, not from the violation list.
Facts before verdicts: show what you found, ask what happened, listen to the answer.
Separate the standard (non-negotiable) from the cause (fixable): two stations at once is a staffing problem wearing a food-safety costume.
End with agreement on what happens before the rush, not with an apology extracted.

misconceptions.misconception: “He knows better — this is a discipline conversation.”
misconceptions.redirect: He does know better, which is the clue: when a skilled person shortcuts, look for the load, not the character.

misconceptions.misconception: “It's faster to just fix it all myself before the rush.”
misconceptions.redirect: Fixing silently fixes today. The conversation is what fixes tomorrow.

phases.label: Walk the Line
phases.purpose: The learner inspects the prep line and names every food-safety violation; the debrief locks all four in standard terms.

practice.purpose: A pre-rush inspection: spot everything wrong on the line, specifically.
practice.label: Spot the violations

when.requirement: Learner names at least three of the four violations as food-safety problems, not tidiness.

exit.final_word: That's the walk. Everything found goes on the list — nothing gets quietly fixed and forgotten.

transition.text: That's the walk. Now line up what's actually here.

exhibit.alt: A commercial kitchen prep line. On the cold rail, a tray of raw chicken sits on the top shelf directly above containers of washed salad greens. Beside it, a clear container of chopped vegetables has no date label. Below the counter, a red sanitizer bucket holds visibly gray, dirty solution. At the end of the line, a hot-holding pan's thermometer needle sits below the 135°F mark.
facts: A tray of raw chicken sits on the shelf directly above containers of ready-to-eat salad greens.
A clear container of chopped vegetables carries no date label.
The sanitizer bucket under the counter holds gray, visibly dirty solution.
The hot-holding pan's thermometer reads below the 135°F line.
The line is otherwise clean and mid-prep; nothing is spilled or burning.

rubric.name: Raw protein above ready-to-eat
rubric.standard_term: Raw chicken stored above ready-to-eat greens — drip cross-contamination; raw proteins store below RTE, always.
rubric.nudge: Look at the cold rail — top shelf versus what's under it.

rubric.name: Unlabeled prep container
rubric.standard_term: A prepped container with no date label — no shelf-life control; every container gets labeled and dated.
rubric.nudge: Check the containers along the rail — what's missing on one of them?

rubric.name: Spent sanitizer solution
rubric.standard_term: A sanitizer bucket with yesterday's solution — spent sanitizer sanitizes nothing; fresh each shift.
rubric.nudge: Look below the counter. What color should that water be?

rubric.name: Hot-holding under temperature
rubric.standard_term: Hot-holding below 135°F — the danger zone; check the gauge, log it, correct it.
rubric.nudge: End of the line — read the gauge on the pan.

brief.text: Forty minutes to the rush. Walk the line end to end and jot every food-safety problem you can see — be specific about what's wrong, not just where.

interaction.jot_placeholder: Name every violation you can spot…

debrief.label: The four violations
debrief.purpose: Credits the catches and locks all four violations in standard terms before the conversation with Marco.
key_points: Raw chicken above ready-to-eat greens — drip cross-contamination; storage order is the control.
No date label — shelf-life control fails silently; label everything, every time.
Spent sanitizer — a dirty bucket cleans nothing while looking like it does.
Hot-holding under 135°F — the danger zone, found by checking, fixed by logging and correcting.
Every one of these was prepped by a specific person under specific pressure — which is the next conversation.
debrief.final_word: Four violations, one line, one person's morning. Now it gets human.

phases.label: Talk to Marco
phases.purpose: The learner raises what they found with the person whose morning it was — standard held, person respected, line fixed before the rush.

practice.purpose: The corrective conversation: facts before verdicts, standard separated from cause, agreement before the rush.

when.requirement: Learner has raised the findings factually without character judgment, surfaced the workload cause, held the standard as non-negotiable, and reached concrete agreement on fixes before the rush.

exit.final_word: The first orders start chattering off the printer. Whatever stands between you and Marco now, the rush is here and the line has to run.

transition.text: That was the conversation that decides how your kitchen runs. Let's take it apart.

interaction.setting: The back of the kitchen, Marco restocking between stations, rush clock ticking.
interaction.emotion_hint: wary — braced for a write-up from the new shift lead

opening_messages.text: Marco sees you coming with your walk-the-line notes and sets down the box he's carrying. The list in your hand reads: raw chicken shelved above the salad greens, a prepped container with no date label, gray spent sanitizer under the counter, and the hot-hold gauge sitting below 135.
Let me guess. You walked my line. Look — I've been running grill AND prep since six, so whatever's on your list, there's a reason for it.

unthoughtful.look_for: Opens with the violation list or a verdict ("four violations, Marco"), threatens a write-up, or lectures on what he already knows.
unthoughtful.response: Marco goes flat and minimal — "okay," "fine," "whatever you say" — complying without engaging.
unthoughtful.progression: The line gets fixed today by order; the shortcut pattern survives untouched, and so does the resentment.

example.learner: Marco, I found four food-safety violations on your line. This is serious — chicken over greens? You know better.
example.reply: Marco's face closes. "Yep. I'll fix it." He turns back to the box and starts stacking, shoulders squared away from you.

neutral.look_for: Leads with respect and the workload, but soft-pedals the standard — the violations become 'stuff to tidy' rather than non-negotiables, or no concrete pre-rush agreement forms.
neutral.response: Marco engages warmly, owns the morning — and negotiates: some of it now, some 'after the rush.'
neutral.progression: Half the line gets fixed now; the hot-hold and the sanitizer drift to 'later,' which the rush will eat.

example.learner: I know you've been carrying two stations, and honestly the line mostly looks great. There are a few things we should sort out when there's a minute.
example.reply: "Appreciate that — it's been a week." Marco half-smiles. "Chicken I can move right now, and I'll do the label with it. Sanitizer and the hot-hold I'll get to after the rush, yeah?"

strong.look_for: Facts before verdicts, workload surfaced as cause, the standard held plainly, and a concrete who-does-what-now agreement — all before the rush.
strong.response: Marco pushes back once with the two-stations reality, hears the standard held anyway, and commits — and the staffing cause goes on the table as its own item.
strong.progression: The line is fixed within minutes, the labels habit gets a system (labels stocked at the station), and Marco leaves the conversation taller, not smaller.

example.learner: Walk it with me for two minutes — I found four things. Before that: you ran two stations alone this morning, and I want to fix THAT too. But the four can't wait: chicken over greens, an undated container, yesterday's sanitizer, and the hot-hold's under 135. What needs to happen before doors?
example.reply: Marco looks at the list, then at you. "Two stations, man." A beat. "...Chicken and the pan I do right now. Bucket's thirty seconds. Put label rolls AT the station and the dating fixes itself." He's already moving.

interaction.input_placeholder: How do you open with Marco?…

debrief.label: Standard held, person kept
debrief.purpose: Ties the inspection and the conversation together: what makes a correction land.
key_points: Facts before verdicts: show the list, don't wield it — the findings are the agenda, not the ammunition.
Name the cause as its own problem: two stations at once is a staffing failure wearing a food-safety costume.
The standard doesn't bend: every violation needs an owner and a before-the-rush deadline, whatever the reason it happened.
Fix the system, not just the instance — a label holder at the station beats a reminder to label.
debrief.final_word: Hold the standard, respect the person, fix the system. All three, every time.

component_groups.title: See it
components: Raw proteins below ready-to-eat, always — storage order is the cross-contamination control.
Every prepped container labeled and dated — shelf-life control fails silently without it.
Fresh sanitizer each shift — spent solution cleans nothing while looking like it does.
Hot-holding at or above 135°F — check the gauge, log it, correct it.

component_groups.title: Say it
components: Open from the person's competence and their morning, never from the violation list.
Show the facts and ask what happened before rendering any verdict.
Hold the standard as non-negotiable while naming the workload cause as its own fixable problem.
Close on a concrete who-does-what-now agreement — and a system change that makes the standard easier to keep.

ideal_response.summary: A pre-rush walk finds the four silent violations — storage order, dating, sanitizer, holding temperature — and the correction that lasts is the one that shows the facts, asks before judging, holds the standard without bending, and fixes the workload system that made the shortcut attractive.
